reference.source: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
clinicalPearls: An anal skin tag is a benign, soft, fibrovascular projection of perianal skin, usually asymptomatic and found incidentally on examination
Tags commonly arise as residua of a previously thrombosed external haemorrhoid, at the site of a healed anal fissure (the sentinel tag/pile), or after anorectal surgery
The chief symptoms, when present, are hygiene difficulty, pruritus ani, and irritation rather than pain or bleeding
A skin tag associated with a chronic anal fissure typically sits at the posterior midline distal to the fissure and signals the underlying fissure rather than being the primary problem
Large, irregular, indurated, or multiple oedematous tags should raise suspicion of Crohn disease, in which characteristic oedematous violaceous tags occur
Management is usually reassurance; excision is offered only for troublesome hygiene, persistent irritation, or diagnostic uncertainty
Excision should be conservative to avoid wound complications and anal stenosis, and any underlying fissure or Crohn disease must be addressed
Histology should be examined after excision to exclude condylomata, intraepithelial neoplasia, or other pathology when appearances are atypical
reference.pathophysiology: Anal skin tags are composed of fibrous and vascular connective tissue covered by squamous epithelium of the anal margin. They most often form when the oedema and stretching of an acute external haemorrhoidal thrombosis resolve, leaving redundant, fibrosed perianal skin. Alternatively, the chronic inflammation and induration of a longstanding anal fissure produce a sentinel tag at the distal fissure margin, or postoperative scarring and healing after anorectal procedures leave residual folds. In Crohn disease, transmural inflammation and lymphatic obstruction generate characteristically oedematous, often broad-based perianal tags. The tags themselves have no malignant potential but can impair local hygiene and provoke secondary irritation and pruritus.
additionalDifferentials: External haemorrhoid or residual thrombosed haemorrhoid
Hypertrophied anal papilla protruding at the anal verge
Anal intraepithelial neoplasia or anal squamous carcinoma
Molluscum contagiosum or other perianal skin lesion
additionalInvestigations: Careful inspection and digital rectal examination of the perianal region
Proctoscopy to assess for associated haemorrhoids or fissure
Examination under anaesthesia where a chronic fissure or Crohn disease is suspected
Histopathological examination of any excised or atypical lesion
Assessment for Crohn disease (bowel symptoms, endoscopy, imaging) when tags are oedematous or multiple
Testing for human papillomavirus-associated disease where warts or neoplasia are suspected
redFlags: Induration, ulceration, or irregularity suggesting anal neoplasia
Multiple oedematous or violaceous tags suggesting Crohn disease
Associated bleeding, discharge, or a non-healing perianal wound
Rapid growth or change in a previously stable lesion
reference.prognosis: Anal skin tags are benign with no malignant potential; they cause no harm and often need no treatment, though when excised for symptoms they heal well provided any underlying fissure or Crohn disease is managed, and can recur if the underlying cause persists.
pitfalls: Excising a sentinel tag without recognising and treating the underlying chronic anal fissure
Aggressive or circumferential excision leading to painful wounds or anal stenosis
Excising oedematous tags in undiagnosed Crohn disease, risking non-healing wounds
Mistaking condylomata or a neoplastic lesion for a simple skin tag and omitting histology
Offering surgery for asymptomatic tags where reassurance would suffice
